title: Further Expansion and Factorisation

findings.finding: Several complete tasks repeat unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The repeated 2ab tasks and expansion tasks have identical expressions and response requirements. The surrounding variation runs suggest useful comparisons, but their prompts do not establish a purpose for solving the unchanged tasks again.
findings.checked: Compared the complete prompts and parent instructions. Guided-practice answers are not student-facing scaffolds. A discernible pattern alone does not satisfy the explicit-purpose exception.
findings.assumptions: The supplied prompts contain the instructional purposes students receive.

repair.proposal: Remove p4-compute-d/e/f, p5-guided-b, p6-q2-a/f, p7-q8-a, p7-q9-a, p7-q10-e and p8-q11-a as repeated solve tasks. In p7-q8, explicitly use the result from p6-q1-c as the baseline for comparing changing coefficients. In p7-q10 and p8-q11, explicitly reuse p7-q9-m as the baseline for their coefficient and sign comparisons, preserving those variation groups.

findings.doneWhen: The named tasks are solved once, and retained comparison baselines explicitly reuse earlier results.

findings.finding: The centred-product demonstration does not explain how its centre and offset are chosen.
findings.breakdown: The working introduces 30 and 3 without modelling the decision needed to construct corresponding brackets independently in parts c and d.
findings.checked: p11 teaches expansion of supplied brackets. p14-q13-a supplies constructed brackets and part b supplies the centre; neither states how to choose the centre.
findings.assumptions: The centred-product method has not been taught separately. Calculator access is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before the working in part a, add: 'Choose the midpoint: (27+33)÷2=30. Each number is 3 from 30, so 27×33=(30−3)(30+3).'

findings.doneWhen: Both constructed numbers are explicitly connected to the original factors.

findings.finding: Question 16 requires reversing the special-product identity before that factorisation method has been taught.
findings.breakdown: Students must recover square bases from fractional, surd and composite terms, whereas the preceding instruction identifies bases inside supplied brackets.
findings.checked: All teaching preceding this question concerns expansion. p14-q10 supplies surd factors, and p14-q12 verifies an area identity by expansion. The explicit reverse method appears later at p29.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary factorisation and surd manipulation may be prior knowledge; reversing this special product still requires instruction here. Calculator access is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Before Question 16, state 'Use the identity backwards: A²−B²=(A−B)(A+B). Identify complete expressions whose squares are the two terms.' Model x²−3/4=x²−(√3/2)²=(x−√3/2)(x+√3/2), explicitly checking the fractional square. Then model (x−2)²−20=(x−2−2√5)(x−2+2√5), retaining x−2 as one expression. Remind students to extract an available common factor first.

findings.doneWhen: Students see the reverse identity and its square-base decisions before independent factorisation.

findings.finding: Two complete expansion tasks recur unchanged in the later practice set.
findings.breakdown: p13-q8-c/d repeat the expressions and required operation in p12-q4-l/m without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.checked: Compared both whole tasks and their parent prompts; no values, givens or scaffolds change.
findings.assumptions: No additional retrieval instruction accompanies these blocks.

repair.proposal: Remove p13-q8-c and p13-q8-d.

findings.doneWhen: Each named expansion task appears once.

findings.finding: Generalise the cancellation in the binomial-trinomial products.
findings.breakdown: Students determine which coefficients eliminate mixed terms rather than only performing the expansion.
findings.checked: Direct expansion gives a³+(k+1)a²b+(l+k)ab²+lb³ and a³+(r−1)a²b+(s−r)ab²−sb³. Cancelling coefficient pairs gives k=−1, l=1 and r=s=1. Only expansion and elementary coefficient equations are needed.
findings.assumptions: The statements are polynomial identities in real variables a and b.

repair.proposal: After p23-bb, ask: 'Find constants k and l so that (a+b)(a²+kab+lb²) has no a²b or ab² terms. Expand to justify your answer. Then find r and s so that (a−b)(a²+rab+sb²) has no mixed terms.' Expected answers: k=−1, l=1, giving a³+b³; r=s=1, giving a³−b³.

findings.doneWhen: An optional task asks students to justify both coefficient choices.

findings.finding: Three perfect-square factorisation tasks repeat unchanged without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The copies of x²+10x+25, x²+6x+9 and 9x²−30x+25 require identical responses.
findings.checked: Compared complete stems, parent instructions and support. p25-guided-a supplies no student-facing completion scaffold; the typesetting changes in the second pair do not change the task.
findings.assumptions: The supplied instructions are complete.

repair.proposal: Remove p26-q1-first-a, p26-q2-a and p26-q2-o. For the positive/negative comparison at the start of Question 1, explicitly reuse the result from p25-guided-a as the positive baseline.

findings.doneWhen: Each named task is solved once, while the sign comparison remains available.

findings.finding: Determine all middle coefficients that make fixed outside terms a perfect-square trinomial.
findings.breakdown: Students explain why both signs are possible and why the middle-term condition excludes other coefficients.
findings.checked: As a polynomial identity, the middle term must be ±2(3x)(4y), so k=±24. For positive A and B, the corresponding condition is k=±2AB. The identification and factorisation methods are taught at p24–p25.
findings.assumptions: Perfect square means the square of a polynomial, with equality for all x and y.

repair.proposal: After p27-q6, ask: 'Find every k for which 9x²+kxy+16y² is a perfect-square trinomial. Factorise each expression and explain why there are no other values. Generalise to A²x²+kxy+B²y², where A,B>0.' Expected answers: k=±24, giving (3x±4y)²; generally k=±2AB, giving (Ax±By)².

findings.doneWhen: An optional task requires both coefficients, both factorisations and their justification.

findings.finding: The closing four-term task requires a grouping strategy that has not yet been taught.
findings.breakdown: The displayed two-term method cannot start on w⁶−w⁴−w²+1. Students must first create matching binomial factors from pairs of terms.
findings.checked: Earlier instruction supplies expansion, special-product factorisation and ordinary common-factor extraction. Grouping expanded four-term expressions is explicitly introduced later at p41.
findings.assumptions: Grouping in pairs is new within the booklet's stated outcomes. Ordinary common-factor extraction is prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: Before part f, model: 'Group terms in pairs to create matching brackets: t³−t²−t+1=t²(t−1)−(t−1)=(t−1)(t²−1)=(t−1)²(t+1).' Then cue part f: 'Group the first two terms and the last two terms.'

findings.doneWhen: Students see how grouping creates a binomial common factor before using it in part f.

findings.finding: Several difference-of-squares tasks repeat unchanged without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The named copies of x²−9, 4x²−25, 4x²−9 and x²−y² have identical expressions and required operations.
findings.checked: Compared complete prompts and givens. The surrounding constant, coefficient and exponent runs have useful variation structures, but their instructions do not explicitly justify repeating these whole tasks.
findings.assumptions: The supplied prompts contain all instructional purposes.

repair.proposal: Remove p30-q3-c, p31-q6-a, p35-q20-a, p31-q5-c, p31-q6-b and p31-q7-a as repeated solve tasks. Preserve their comparison positions with explicit directions to reuse the earlier factorisations as reference results when comparing the changed constants, coefficients or exponents.

findings.doneWhen: The unchanged tasks are solved once and the variation runs explicitly reuse their baselines.

findings.finding: Generalise repeated difference-of-squares factorisation for powers that double.
findings.breakdown: Students explain the repeated halving of the exponent and predict the resulting factors.
findings.checked: Repeated use of the identity gives x⁸−1=(x−1)(x+1)(x²+1)(x⁴+1), and adds x⁸+1 for x¹⁶−1. For every positive integer n, the general product is (x−1) times the factors x^(2^j)+1 for j=0 through n−1. This uses the exponent patterns and repeated factorisation already encountered.
findings.assumptions: The requested factors have integer coefficients; the general statement is a polynomial identity.

repair.proposal: After p35-q22, ask: 'Factorise x⁸−1 and x¹⁶−1 using integer coefficients. Predict the corresponding factorisation of x^(2^n)−1 for positive integer n, and explain the process.' Expected answers: (x−1)(x+1)(x²+1)(x⁴+1); the same product with (x⁸+1); generally (x−1)(x+1)(x²+1)…(x^(2^(n−1))+1), because each remaining difference factor has its exponent halved.

findings.doneWhen: An optional task includes the two cases and an explained generalisation.

findings.finding: Three complete binomial-common-factor tasks repeat unchanged without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copies have the same expressions, required responses and support. Question 3's sign variants suggest a comparison, but its prompt does not establish that purpose for the repeated baseline.
findings.checked: Compared all three pairs and their parent prompts. Both targeted guided-practice items are unscaffolded.
findings.assumptions: No separate retrieval instruction accompanies the copies.

repair.proposal: Remove p38-q3-a, p38-q4-d and p38-q4-i as solve tasks. Before p38-q3-b–d, explicitly direct students to use p38-q2-c as their reference and predict how changing signs changes the second factor.

findings.doneWhen: Each task is solved once and Question 3 retains an explicit positive-sign baseline.

findings.finding: The grouping topic does not rehearse numerical and algebraic monomial HCF extraction from expanded pairs.
findings.breakdown: Both examples require students to generate matching brackets by extracting factors such as 3x, 2 and 3y. Remembering visible binomial extraction alone does not supply fluent recall of this step.
findings.checked: p36's review divides individual terms. p37's expanded-pair examples mainly extract 1 or −1. The preceding binomial-factor exercise does not practise numerical and algebraic HCF extraction from expanded pairs throughout.
findings.assumptions: Monomial HCF factorisation is prior knowledge. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Add four short opening items: 'Factorise by taking out the HCF: (a) 6y+9; (b) 4y+6; (c) 6xy+9x; (d) 6y−3xy.' Expected answers: 3(2y+3), 2(2y+3), 3x(2y+3), 3y(2−x).

findings.doneWhen: A short review rehearses both numerical and variable HCF extraction before the examples.

findings.finding: The complete grouping task x²+4x+3x+12 is repeated without an explicit comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copy changes neither expression nor support. The surrounding sign pattern does not itself instruct students to compare with the earlier task.
findings.checked: Compared both whole prompts and parent instructions; both are unscaffolded factorisation tasks.
findings.assumptions: No additional comparison instruction accompanies Question 3.

repair.proposal: Remove p43-q3-a as a solve task. Direct students to reuse p43-q2-b as the positive-sign baseline and predict the effects of the sign changes in p43-q3-b–d.

findings.doneWhen: The expression is solved once and its result explicitly anchors the sign comparison.

findings.finding: The non-monic topic uses signed factor-pair retrieval without an opening rehearsal.
findings.breakdown: The example immediately requires two integers satisfying both a product and a sum. Incorrect signs or checking only one condition prevents the middle-term split.
findings.checked: There is no opening review. The preceding grouping review and exercise do not require searching for signed integers satisfying simultaneous product and sum conditions.
findings.assumptions: Signed factor-pair selection is prior knowledge, consistent with the separate monic-quadratic booklet. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Add: 'Find two integers with product P and sum S. Check both conditions: (a) P=12, S=7; (b) P=12, S=−7; (c) P=−12, S=1; (d) P=−12, S=−1.' Expected pairs: 3,4; −3,−4; 4,−3; 3,−4.

findings.doneWhen: A short review rehearses positive, negative and mixed-sign pairs before the example.

findings.finding: All four solve tasks in Question 6 repeat earlier complete factorisation tasks without an explicit purpose.
findings.breakdown: The expressions and response requirements are unchanged. The fixed-factor pattern is useful, but 'Factorise' does not explicitly establish a comparison with earlier results.
findings.checked: Compared all four pairs and parent instructions. Removing earlier copies would disrupt existing sign or coefficient runs.
findings.assumptions: An unstated teacher comparison does not justify repetition in the supplied booklet.

repair.proposal: Remove p52-q6a–d as repeated solve tasks. Preserve the fixed-factor comparison with: 'Collect your factorisations from Question 3(a), Question 3(e), Question 4(a) and Question 5(b). What factor stays the same, and how does the other factor change?'

findings.doneWhen: The four tasks are solved once and their results are explicitly reused for comparison.

findings.finding: Generalise the fixed-factor pattern and explain its middle coefficient.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the factor-pair procedure to expansion and explain why one factor remains unchanged.
findings.checked: (nx+1)(x+4)=nx²+(4n+1)x+4 for every positive integer n. Substituting n=7 gives 7x²+29x+4. Both expansion and factorisation methods are available.
findings.assumptions: The generalisation is a polynomial identity in x, with positive integer n.

repair.proposal: After p52-q5, ask: 'Factorise nx²+(4n+1)x+4 for any positive integer n and explain why it works. Predict the expression and factors when n=7.' Expected answer: (nx+1)(x+4), justified by expansion; 7x²+29x+4=(7x+1)(x+4).

findings.doneWhen: An optional task includes the general factors, their explanation and the n=7 prediction.

findings.finding: The method-selection chart directs every residual two-term expression to difference of squares without testing its applicability.
findings.breakdown: After HCF extraction, b−25 and 16−g are already fully factorised over rational coefficients. The chart nevertheless directs students to a method whose square-term condition they fail.
findings.checked: p28 and p29 teach the necessary square-term condition, but the permanently visible consolidation chart omits that decision and immediately encounters counterexamples.
findings.assumptions: Students use the chart to select among the taught methods.

repair.proposal: Qualify the two-term branch: 'Use difference of squares only when both terms are squares and they are subtracted. Otherwise check whether the expression is already fully factorised.'

findings.doneWhen: The chart includes the applicability test and permits stopping after HCF extraction.

findings.finding: The required HCF-first instruction does not provide a feasible starting step for part i.
findings.breakdown: The four displayed terms in ax²−a−2x²+2 have no nontrivial common factor. Grouping must first expose the common binomial.
findings.checked: Grouping is already taught at p41, but that knowledge does not make the question's prescribed first step available as written.
findings.assumptions: Students follow the explicit first-step instruction.

repair.proposal: Beside part i, add: 'For this part, group in pairs first to expose a binomial common factor.'

findings.doneWhen: The part supplies a feasible starting instruction while leaving the grouping and factorisation to students.

findings.finding: The complete task of factorising 2x²−18 repeats unchanged.
findings.breakdown: The later copy changes no values, givens, support or required operation and has no explicit retrieval purpose.
findings.checked: Compared both whole tasks and parent prompts; both independently request factorisation.
findings.assumptions: The supplied instructions are complete.

repair.proposal: Remove p59-q5-b.

findings.doneWhen: Only p57-q2-t retains this complete task.

findings.finding: The first general quartic trinomial requires recognising a quadratic in x² without preceding instruction supplying that representation.
findings.breakdown: Students need to reinterpret x⁴−5x²+4 before applying the taught quadratic factorisation procedure.
findings.checked: p25-guided-f uses the special perfect-square pattern with a higher-power base; p63-q6 uses two-term differences of squares. Neither supplies the general quadratic-in-x² route.
findings.assumptions: The taught quadratic methods are known, but disguised-quadratic substitution has not been taught separately.

repair.proposal: Before part a, add: 'Let t=x². Then x⁴−5x²+4=t²−5t+4. Factorise in t, replace t by x², then check whether the factors can be factorised further.'

findings.doneWhen: Students have an explicit route to the familiar quadratic method and back.

findings.finding: Two complete repeated-factorisation tasks recur in the challenge exercise without an explicit retrieval purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copies of x⁴−16 and x⁸−1 have unchanged givens and require the same factorisations.
findings.checked: Compared the complete tasks and parent prompts. The later identity reminder supplies no changed scaffold or distinct response requirement, and does not establish a retrieval purpose.

contextQuestions.question: Have students previously learned to justify divisibility algebraically using integer multiples and parity, including explaining why products of consecutive integers contain the required factors? Earlier challenge prompts connect consecutive odd integers with 2n−1 and 2n+1, but do not establish this broader proof method; the answer would determine whether the later proof tasks need teaching or a reordered introductory sequence.
